title: Haggai 1:1–11
context: Haggai’s first oracle is dated to the first day of the sixth month in the second year of Darius the king (1:1), a date commonly placed in 520 BC. The LORD’s word comes through Haggai the prophet to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest. The people have returned from exile, but the LORD’s house still lies waste while they live in “paneled houses” (1:4). The LORD twice calls them to “Consider your ways” (1:5, 1:7), describes harvests and wages that never satisfy (1:6, 1:9–11), and commands them to bring wood and build (1:8). Ezra 5:1–2 and 6:14 also record Haggai’s preaching alongside Zechariah’s and the rebuilding under Zerubbabel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak; each account can be read in its own place. Shared ground: both traditions read the passage as a call to put the LORD’s presence and worship first. Neither reads the drought as a promise that obedience earns wealth; the hardship is covenant discipline that calls the people back to the LORD.

verses.text: In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, in the first day of the month, the LORD’s word came by Haggai the prophet, to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The date, “In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, in the first day of the month”, sets the oracle in the Persian period after the return. Arminian readers note that the LORD’s word comes to named leaders, who are responsible to lead the people in answering it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD addressing Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, the civil and priestly leaders of the restored community. Shared ground: both traditions read the dated heading as placing the word of the LORD in real history, and both see leadership as carrying a particular duty to hear and obey.

verses.text: “This is what the LORD of Armies says: These people say, ‘The time hasn’t yet come, the time for the LORD’s house to be built.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies reports the people’s own words: “The time hasn’t yet come”. Arminian readers hear a real excuse freely chosen, which postpones obedience and calls for a real change of mind.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear an excuse that treats delay as prudence while neglecting the LORD’s house. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as exposing a common temptation to wait for better circumstances before honoring God, and both hear the LORD naming the excuse in order to correct it.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s word came by Haggai the prophet, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator notes, “Then the LORD’s word came by Haggai the prophet”. Arminian readers see the LORD answering the people’s excuse with a fresh word, giving them a new opportunity to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD taking the initiative to speak again through his prophet, who carries a message not his own. Shared ground: both traditions read the short heading as underscoring that Haggai speaks with the LORD’s authority, and that what follows is the LORD’s answer to 1:2.

verses.text: “Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies waste?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks, “Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies waste?” Arminian readers hear a searching question that invites the people to weigh their priorities and choose differently.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a rebuke of misplaced priorities, with the contrast between the people’s houses and the LORD’s house exposing their hearts. Shared ground: both traditions read the question as a call to put the LORD’s worship before private comfort, not as a condemnation of homes as such.

verses.text: Now therefore this is what the LORD of Armies says: ‘Consider your ways.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says, “Consider your ways.” Arminian readers hear a call to honest reflection that the people can and must answer, looking at their own conduct in the light of the LORD’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a summons to self-examination under God’s word, which the Spirit uses to bring conviction and amendment. Shared ground: both traditions read the call as the hinge of the oracle, repeated in 1:7, and as a model of repentance that begins with looking honestly at one’s ways.

verses.text: You have sown much, and bring in little. You eat, but you don’t have enough. You drink, but you aren’t filled with drink. You clothe yourselves, but no one is warm; and he who earns wages earns wages to put them into a bag with holes in it.’
verses.arminianNotes: “You have sown much, and bring in little.” Arminian readers hear the futility of labor that leaves the LORD out, pictured in wages put “into a bag with holes in it”, and they read it as discipline meant to turn the people back, not as a formula for wealth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see covenant discipline in harvests and wages that never satisfy, recalling the warnings of the law. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the people’s restlessness had a spiritual root, and both resist reading it as a promise that giving to God secures prosperity.

verses.text: “This is what the LORD of Armies says: ‘Consider your ways.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies repeats, “Consider your ways.” Arminian readers hear the repetition as the LORD’s patience, pressing the same call again so that the people will finally respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the repeated call as emphasis, leading from diagnosis in 1:6 to command in 1:8. Shared ground: both traditions read the repetition as marking the turn from exposing the people’s situation to telling them what to do, with the same call to honest self-examination.

verses.text: Go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build the house. I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD commands, “Go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build the house.” Arminian readers hear a plain, doable command and a gracious promise: “I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified”.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the command joined to the LORD’s own purpose, that he be glorified in his house. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the point of rebuilding is the LORD’s pleasure and glory, not the building’s size or splendor, and both hear the command as something the people are able to begin at once.

verses.text: “You looked for much, and, behold, it came to little; and when you brought it home, I blew it away. Why?” says the LORD of Armies, “Because of my house that lies waste, while each of you is busy with his own house.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says, “You looked for much, and, behold, it came to little”. Arminian readers hear the LORD explaining the people’s hardship as the result of their choice to be “busy with his own house” while his house lies waste.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s hand behind the failed harvests: “I blew it away.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as tying the people’s disappointment to their neglect of the LORD’s house, while reading it as covenant discipline for this setting rather than a rule that every hardship has a hidden cause.

verses.text: Therefore for your sake the heavens withhold the dew, and the earth withholds its fruit.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore for your sake the heavens withhold the dew, and the earth withholds its fruit.” Arminian readers hear the covenant warnings of the law at work, with creation itself answering the people’s neglect.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s providence over rain and harvest, governing creation for the good of his people even when that means discipline. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a covenant setting, in which the land’s barrenness serves as a call to return rather than a sign that the LORD has abandoned them.

verses.text: I called for a drought on the land, on the mountains, on the grain, on the new wine, on the oil, on that which the ground produces, on men, on livestock, and on all the labor of the hands.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I called for a drought on the land”. Arminian readers see judgment that touches every part of life, from grain and oil to “all the labor of the hands”, and that aims to bring the people to reconsider their ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s sovereign hand in the drought, sent as a fatherly discipline on a covenant people. Shared ground: both traditions read the drought as the LORD’s call to the people to put him first again, and both resist turning the oracle into a promise that obedience brings guaranteed material reward.
